documents.abstract: The study draws on two complementary data sources. The quantitative data come from a cross-sectional online survey administered to university students enrolled in Turkish higher education institutions. Stratified random sampling ensures representation across institutional types. The strata include metropolitan foundation universities, metropolitan public universities, and provincial state universities. The survey instrument uses validated scales adapted from prior research on Technology Continuance Theory and GenAI adoption. All items are measured on a five-point Likert scale. The constructs measured include Perceived Ease of Use, Perceived Usefulness, Confirmation, Satisfaction, Trust, Perceived Security, Continuance Intention, and Use. Trust items measure confidence in the AI tools. One item asks whether students trust GenAI tools to provide accurate information. Another asks whether students trust developers to prevent unethical use of student data. The survey does not measure trust in university administration. The survey is available in Turkish and English. Translation follows a rigorous protocol. The research team drafts the survey in English, translates it into Turkish, and back-translates it into English. Native speakers review both versions for clarity, cultural accuracy, and linguistic equivalence.The qualitative data come from semi-structured interviews with academics. Purposive sampling recruits academics across three institutional strata. The strata are elite foundation universities in Istanbul, major public universities in Ankara, and provincial state universities in eastern and southeastern Türkiye. The sample also includes academics from Northern Cyprus, transnational institutions, and the Turkish and Kurdish diaspora. The interview protocol explores GenAI use in teaching and research, perceptions of institutional support, experiences with infrastructure limitations, views on domestic AI models, and intentions regarding academic migration. The protocol includes specific probes for Kurdish academics and academics at conservative foundation universities. The interview guide is drafted in English and translated into Turkish and Kurdish. Native speakers review both translations. Back-translation ensures linguistic equivalence. Interviews are conducted in Turkish, Kurdish, or English based on participant preference. Interviews are audio-recorded with participant consent and transcribed verbatim.Data analysis uses Generalized Structured Component Analysis in SmartPLS 4.0 for the quantitative phase. Preliminary data screening uses SPSS 28. Screening includes tests for normality, multicollinearity, and common method bias. The qualitative phase uses WEBQDA for digital coding. The coding framework includes deductive codes from Technology Continuance Theory and inductive codes that emerge from the data. Deductive codes include Perceived Usefulness, Perceived Ease of Use, Satisfaction, Trust in AI tools, Perceived Security, and Continuance Intention. Inductive codes include Institutional Trust, Infrastructure Context, Diaspora and Academic Retention, and Domestic AI Sovereignty. The research team builds a code co-occurrence matrix to trace links between institutional trust and trust in AI tools.Ethical approval comes from the Ethics Committee of CEOS.PP at the Polytechnic Institute of Porto. Data collection follows the Turkish Personal Data Protection Law and the General Data Protection Regulation. Participants receive information sheets and provide written informed consent. All data are anonymised upon collection. Participants receive alphanumeric codes that indicate region and institutional type but do not reveal individual identities. Audio recordings are deleted after transcription. Transcripts are stored on an encrypted, password-protected server accessible only to the research team. Data are retained for five years and then permanently deleted.

Advances in generative AI are opening new opportunities for mathematics learning in higher education, but systematic mapping of the Theory–Context–Methodology (TCM) framework to integrate generative AI into mathematics learning remains limited. This study aims to identify the theories or conceptual frameworks, application contexts, and research methods used in studies of generative AI in higher education mathematics education. The method used is a PRISMA-based systematic literature review. The search was conducted on Scopus, Lens, and Dimensions, yielding 322 initial articles; after deduplication, screening, and eligibility assessment, 31 articles were analyzed. Article quality was assessed using the MMAT, while data were analyzed through TCM-based coding. The results indicate that generative AI is conceptualized as a pedagogical tool, a technology adoption, pedagogical competence, mathematical activity, and a cognitive partner. Its application is dominant in the classroom, general mathematics, ChatGPT, and for conceptual understanding. Methodologically, the studies were dominated by qualitative and quantitative approaches, while mixed methods and R&D/development research remained limited. These findings underscore the need for AI-based instructional designs that are critical, ethical, and supported by more integrative empirical research.

documents.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Large Language Models in Higher Education: Applications, Challenges, Ethical Concerns, and Future Directions explores the growing role of generative artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs) in transforming higher education. The book examines their applications in teaching, learning, research, academic writing, assessment, and personalized education. It highlights how AI-powered tools can support educators, enhance student engagement, improve access to learning resources, and facilitate academic productivity. At the same time, it addresses key challenges, including academic dishonesty, data privacy, algorithmic bias, misinformation, and the potential overdependence on AI-generated content. The book also discusses ethical considerations, institutional policies, responsible AI use, and the importance of maintaining human judgment in educational practices. Furthermore, it explores future directions, emerging technologies, and strategies for integrating AI into higher education effectively. This book is a valuable resource for educators, researchers, students, academic administrators, and policymakers interested in understanding and responsibly adopting AI-driven educational innovations.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) recently appeared as an issue of its time which has been changing the educational landscape at a considerable rate and opening new pathways and challenges for educators and learners. Therefore, in terms of GenAI for education this bibliometric analysis will characterize the change and development by mapping trends and patterns, examining prevalent subject areas in academia interest. Following the established criteria, we ran a systematic search on Scopus database with the identification and analysis of 121 peer-reviewed documents (journal articles, review articles and conference papers; selection reported with reference to the PRISMA 2020 guideline) published between January 2023 and March 2025 related to GenAI applied in education. The thematic labels attached to the algorithmically generated VOSviewer clusters were assigned by the researchers, and interpretations of regional patterns are presented as tentative. The article features papers discussing ways to use GenAI in learner-centered teaching, curriculum development and assessment. The findings reveal a rapid increase in research output between 2023 (23 articles) and 2024 (67 articles), followed by 31 articles in the first quarter of 2025, and substantial international collaboration (34% of the articles). Moreover, the thematic analysis shows that pedagogical integration and instructional design (55.4% of the articles), assessment and academic integrity (44.6%) and ethical and societal implications (39.7%) are the most prominent themes, with a shift from ethical and assessment concerns in 2023 towards pedagogical integration and learning outcomes in 2024-2025. Research affiliated with the United States, the United Kingdom, China and Germany dominates the corpus, whereas research from Latin America and Africa appears under-represented. The review proposes future directions of research and spells out an array of issues that have until now gone unexamined by helping the reader enter the intellectual landscape of GenAI in education. The bibliometric evidence indicates growing scholarly attention to the potential of GenAI in education; this study did not appraise the quality of the evidence on learning outcomes. Nonetheless, designers are being asked to collectively conduct further research to address any potential negative effects of the technology, and create useful design frameworks, to implement this technology into the education system worldwide, without compromising on justice and morality.

documents.abstract: Research Software Engineering (RSEng) is grounded in the belief that better, higher-quality software enables better research. As we look to the future of RSEng, we see that generative AI could substantially accelerate and expand the scope of research software development, but it also fundamentally shifts the nature of research software development by making code easier to generate than to understand, validate, or maintain. This is especially consequential in scientific computing, where software quality is directly tied to reproducibility, trust, and scientific validity. For RSEs, there is now an urgent need to advance a practical vision for how we will succeed in producing high-quality, trustworthy software under these new circumstances. We argue that in the age of AI for science, developers play an essential role in creating quality by reasoning about, negotiating, and ensuring it across the software lifecycle. We advance a theory that helps explain what, exactly, developers contribute by focusing on three constructs: values, which shape which quality attributes matter; expertise, which enables individuals to pursue and evaluate those attributes; and collaboration, which coordinates diverse forms of knowledge and accountability. To both build better AI tools for research software development and prepare our workforce, we need to better understand which values, what kinds of expertise, and what forms of collaboration will prove most helpful. For that, we seek expert input from Research Software Engineers(RSEs). This poster provides participants with an entertaining, interactive experience with the core ideas of our research. As well as sharing the preliminary thoughts and opinions gathered from an interview study that is currently underway. This interview study was motivated by the work this poster is highlighting. By showing the preliminary results we hope to initiate a dialog with RSEs. As such invite the audience to reflect on what quality means in their own practice, and the work that is needed to achieve it in concert with AI. Attendees can contribute responses on post-it notes attached to the poster and will be invited to continue the conversation through a survey. We will encourage those who wish to learn more about our team’s ongoing work on these topics to attend our talk "We Create Quality: Towards a Human-Centric Theory of Research Software Quality in the Age of AI”.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) provides students with rapid access to explanations, summaries, and suggested answers. For 15-year-old learners, this accessibility raises an important educational and behavioural question: under what circumstances does AI support meaningful engagement with challenging learning materials, and when might it reduce opportunities for independent cognitive effort? This paper reviews published research in behavioural science and selected findings from the OECD's PISA 2025 Results (Volume I), with particular emphasis on Uzbekistan. Cognitive-demand avoidance and cognitive offloading are employed as theoretical frameworks for interpreting patterns of AI use, while a clear distinction is maintained between these concepts and the variables directly measured by PISA. According to the OECD, 48.6% of students in Uzbekistan use AI chatbots at least once a week to support their learning, compared with the OECD average of 45.5%. Furthermore, 80.6% of students in Uzbekistan report learning at school how to evaluate AI-generated information, compared with an OECD average of 62.6% (OECD, 2026). These findings indicate that AI-assisted learning is already widespread among students. However, the reported figures do not establish how frequently students substitute AI-generated summaries for assigned reading materials or identify the motivations underlying individual decisions to use AI in this way. The paper argues that the educational implications of AI use depend on the nature of the cognitive tasks delegated to AI, the learner's objectives, and the extent to which AI-generated information is critically evaluated and integrated into independent learning. As the study relies on secondary sources and does not involve the analysis of individual-level student records or the collection of primary empirical data, the proposed explanations should be understood as theoretically informed interpretations rather than established causal relationships. The paper concludes that educational institutions should develop students' ability not only to use AI tools effectively but also to recognise when independent reading, source verification, and critical reasoning remain essential for meaningful learning.

documents.abstract: The educational value of artificial intelligence (AI) depends on technological capabilities and human–AI interaction. This is particularly relevant in interpreter training, which involves high cognitive demands, contextual decisions, and time-sensitive activities. This study examines how Human-Centred Artificial Intelligence (HCAI) principles can guide AI-assisted educational environments for interpreter training. Using Design Science Research (DSR), an environment integrating AI capabilities across the training cycle was developed and evaluated. Drawing on literature concerning Computer-Assisted Interpreting, HCAI, human–AI interaction, technology acceptance, and interpreting cognition, five design principles were derived: learner agency and human control, transparency and calibrated trust, protection of cognitive resources, contextualised assistance, and AI as a support for learning. A technology acceptance study involving 42 professional interpreters provided contextual evidence on technology use, adoption barriers, and professional practice, informing the specification of these principles. The principles were operationalised in the artefact, and its interaction design was examined through formative heuristic evaluation. Professional evidence therefore informs the design without establishing learner-centred validation or educational effectiveness. The contribution is a human-centred, professionally informed framework linking literature, contextual evidence, design requirements, and implementation to align AI capabilities with educational objectives and the cognitive and interactional demands of interpreter training through explicit and traceable design decisions.

documents.abstract: Abstract Shifting technological landscapes have been shaping the epistemologies, methods, and workflows of classicists, historians, and archaeologists for more than a century. Yet these technologies and their impacts have not always been subject to reflexive interrogation within our disciplines. As artificial intelligence (AI) technologies – especially generative AI – have become widely accessible, there has been a wave of concern among educators around student learning outcomes and academic honesty. In addressing these challenges, we must also engage in critical reflection around the use of AI technologies in our research and teaching from humanist and social scientist perspectives in order to serve critical learning outcomes and counter rising digital colonialism. This paper first situates the conversation within the context of corporate AI economies and the intersections between AI technologies and antiquity-focused fields. It then proposes three AI-focused literacies for cultivating core ancient Mediterranean studies competencies and fostering critical thinking: the ability to identify and analyse the impact of taxonomic frameworks and data training inputs on algorithmic outputs; the ability to understand the development of computational models and algorithmic reasoning and their applications; and the ability to critically evaluate the ethical and environmental impacts of algorithmic reasoning and AI technologies. Critical assessment of the foundational structures and logics of AI systems and economies situates both educators and learners to critically assess the political, social, and environmental impacts of such systems on the study of the past and the world in the present.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-generated creative exemplars are increasingly used as scalable digital instructional resources in creativity education. However, it remains unclear whether labeling identical exemplars as human- or AI-generated shapes how learners engage in group creative activities. We tested this possibility in 113 dyads using an fNIRS hyperscanning group creative ideation paradigm. Dyads completed creative ideation tasks before, during, and after exemplar-stimulation. During stimulation, the human- and AI-attribution groups received identical exemplars labeled as produced by human or AI, whereas the control group received no exemplar. Human attribution increased idea uniqueness during stimulation relative to both the other phases and the AI-attribution and control groups. AI attribution temporarily increased switching among ideation pathways. Neither behavioral effect persisted after exemplar withdrawal. The two attribution groups did not differ in exemplar-category overlap or nearest-exemplar semantic distance, but human-attribution dyads rated the exemplars as more helpful. Human attribution also increased interbrain synchronization (IBS) in bilateral premotor and supplementary motor cortices during stimulation, whereas AI attribution was associated with decreased IBS in the left supramarginal gyrus and right frontopolar cortex from pre- to post-stimulation. Thus, exemplar-source attribution shapes the process and outcome of group creative ideation, revealing an important social-contextual factor in AI-supported creativity education.

documents.abstract: Job burnout has become a central concern in organizational behavior, human resource management, and occupational health psychology. Although it is frequently discussed as a problem of excessive workload, contemporary scholarship conceptualizes burnout as a multidimensional response to chronic, unsuccessfully managed occupational stress. This narrative review synthesizes foundational theories, meta-analyses, measurement research, and selected recent developments to clarify what burnout is, why it emerges, how it affects workers and organizations, and which interventions appear promising. Particular attention is given to the job demands–resources framework, conservation of resources theory, emotional labor, the recovery process, and mismatches between employees and their workplaces. The review also examines ongoing debates concerning burnout's overlap with depression, alternative measurement instruments, the limitations of predominantly cross-sectional evidence, and the risks of treating individual resilience as a substitute for organizational change. Finally, it develops a research agenda concerning digital work, artificial intelligence, work–nonwork boundaries, withdrawal behaviors, and multilevel processes. The central argument is that burnout is best understood as a dynamic outcome of the interaction between working conditions and employees' capacity to sustain and replenish psychological resources. Research and management practice should consequently prioritize the redesign of work as well as appropriate individual support.

documents.abstract: Immersive virtual reality (IVR) has shown positive effects on second language (L2) learning, yet the mechanisms underlying these effects remain unclear. Based on the Cognitive Affective Model of Immersive Learning (CAMIL), the present study used structural equation modeling to examine how affective (situational interest, intrinsic motivation, emotions) and cognitive variables (cognitive load, embodied learning, self-efficacy) contribute to receptive L2 vocabulary learning through IVR. A group of native Chinese speakers was asked to learn Korean words in an IVR environment. They were then administered a lexical recognition task that measured learning outcomes. The results revealed two sequences of associations through which IVR affected vocabulary recognition performance: a cognitive path that intersected with presence and self-efficacy; and an affective path that intersected with presence and emotions. Situational interest and intrinsic motivation also demonstrated a sequence of associations with receptive L2 vocabulary recognition. Although further independent confirmation is needed, these findings put forth theoretically meaningful patterns regarding the cognitive-affective mechanisms of IVR-based L2 learning.

Assessment is most powerful when understood as a leadership-driven process of continuous improvement—iterative, evidence-informed, and oriented toward genuine learning rather than compliance. However, the coordination costs of meaningful assessment have historically exceeded most programs’ capacity to sustain it. This paper examines how generative artificial intelligence, and in particular retrieval-augmented reasoning environments, can function as leadership-support tools that change the conditions under which assessment becomes practically feasible without displacing the human judgment it requires. Drawing on leadership education and assessment scholarship, we develop a three-level framework—individual and course, program, and institutional—and present six practice-based use cases illustrating AI-supported assessment at each level, including an AI-populated curriculum alignment matrix and an AI-assisted synthesis of external program reviews. We also directly address the tensions practitioners must navigate: data contamination from AI-generated student work, reliability-validity trade-offs, the limitations of AI detection tools, and the faculty professional development gap. Implications for assessment leaders are discussed.

Background: Concerns that humans may become overly reliant on technologies that support or perform cognitive tasks long predate contemporary artificial intelligence (AI). Across successive generations of cognitive technologies, scholars have examined related concerns through distinct research traditions, each bringing its own assumptions, concepts, and vocabulary to the problem. Existing reviews have generally focused on specific manifestations of over-reliance, leaving limited understanding of how these bodies of scholarship relate to one another. This meta-narrative review examines how different research traditions have conceptualized over-reliance on cognitive technologies and what recurring patterns and broader insights emerge across traditions and as these technologies have evolved. Methods: We apply the meta-narrative method through six iterative phases: planning, searching, mapping, appraisal, synthesis, and recommendations. The search combines exploratory scoping, a structured search of Web of Science Core Collection and ProQuest, and backward and forward citation tracing. The mapping phase will identify historically and intellectually coherent research traditions and trace their development over time. Studies will be appraised according to the quality criteria of their respective traditions and analyzed to reconstruct how each tradition has conceptualized, explained, and investigated over-reliance. The synthesis will compare the resulting meta-narratives to identify recurring patterns and points of convergence, divergence, and tension. The recommendations phase will provide a research agenda and consider implications for research and practice. Discussion: By bringing distinct bodies of scholarship into conversation, this review seeks to build a more cumulative understanding of over-reliance on cognitive technologies. It may help distinguish longstanding problems of over-reliance from those more specific to contemporary AI, recover insights developed in relation to earlier technologies, and identify unresolved tensions and questions. These insights may inform research and efforts to design, implement, and govern cognitive technologies in ways that preserve human judgment and expertise in professional practice.

documents.abstract: Multi-agent systems driven by large language models (LLMs) rely on structured communication topologies to facilitate information exchange and collaborative reasoning. However, effectively scheduling these topologies to dynamically determine who talks to whom and when to communicate remains a fundamental challenge in balancing collective reasoning performance against exponential token overhead. Existing topology scheduling approaches either enforce static communication graphs that cannot adapt to dynamic problem-solving states, or overlook agent role complementarity while failing to explicitly incorporate the synthesized graph structure into team-level decision evaluation. To tackle these limitations, we propose ACTS, a role-aware adaptive communication topology scheduling framework for efficient LLM multi-agent collaboration. Orchestrated within a Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE) paradigm, ACTS introduces a novel dual-attention mechanism. Specifically, a Role-conditioned Relational Attention module dynamically selects variable-cardinality interaction partners based on agent roles and evolving execution states, while a Topological Attention Mixer explicitly embeds the directed communication topology into team value decomposition for precise credit assignment. Comprehensive evaluations across 9 challenging benchmarks covering code generation, multi-step reasoning, general knowledge, and competitive mathematics demonstrate that ACTS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, boosting average accuracy by up to 6.19 percentage points while reducing token consumption by over 15%. The project website is available at https://acts-mas.github.io/ACTS/.

documents.abstract: This study examines the relationships between research motivation and scientific research performance among faculty in teaching–research-oriented universities in China. Based on survey data from 329 faculty members, confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling were used to examine the associations between intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, avoidance motivation, and six dimensions of scientific research performance: Scientific Research Projects (RPJ), Academic Papers (PUB), Monographs (MON), Scientific Research Awards (AWA), Consultation and Decision-making Results (POL), and Technology Transfer Outputs (TRF). The findings indicate that avoidance motivation was positively associated with RPJ, PUB, and POL. Extrinsic motivation was positively associated with RPJ and TRF, whereas intrinsic motivation was positively associated with PUB, MON, and AWA. Overall, the findings show that different forms of research motivation are associated with different performance domains. Within this multidimensional framework, the study offers a context-sensitive reconsideration of avoidance motivation as an active but controlled and potentially performance-relevant orientation under strong institutional accountability.

documents.abstract: Marine fishing is a high-risk occupation that sustains the livelihoods of coastal communities worldwide. This study highlights the occupational hazards associated with marine fishing, drawing on an empirical case study of the high-intensity, multi-day offshore fishing sector in southern India. Following the FAO/ILO/IMO joint framework on occupational health and safety of fishers, our research revealed significant deficiencies in the adoption of safety devices, communication technologies, and navigation systems by sample fishers in the study areas. These gaps, compounded by weak regulatory enforcement and low insurance coverage, pose substantial risks, exacerbated by climate change. The findings underscore the need for targeted interventions—including awareness campaigns, training, and financial aid—to foster a robust safety culture and mitigate economic barriers, leading to improved fisher safety and well-being in the coastal regions of India.

documents.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), particularly large language models such as ChatGPT, has reshaped academic workflows while raising questions about trust, misconceptions, and future expectations. This study examines an integrated framework grounded in the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology and the technology acceptance model to assess how foundational acceptance drivers, cognitive evaluations, misconceptions, and trust are associated with academics’ forward-looking expectations of ChatGPT. Survey data from 252 academics in Malaysian public and private universities were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modelling. Performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and facilitating conditions were positively associated with perceived ease of use (PEOU) or perceived usefulness (PU), while PEOU was positively associated with trust. Social influence was not significantly associated with PU. Two unexpected patterns were observed: PU was positively associated with misconceptions, and misconceptions were positively associated with trust. These cross-sectional associations suggest that functional appreciation can coexist with inflated capability beliefs and potentially miscalibrated trust, but they do not establish a causal mechanism of belief amplification. The Malaysian setting is analytically relevant because higher education institutions are expanding digitalization while national initiatives increasingly emphasize responsible AI governance, institutional capability, and digital skills. The findings highlight the importance of AI literacy, transparent institutional guidance, verification practices, and calibrated reliance when integrating GenAI into higher education.

documents.abstract: Abstract For the health sector, novel applications involving automated decision-making (ADM) and artificial intelligence (AI) are seen as a way to fill critical gaps in health systems and improve patient care and outcomes. For patients, carers, and health consumers more broadly, these innovations may be viewed as a way to improve their agency and understanding of their bodies and health states. Yet, many of the devices and software remain speculative or in limited pilot testing. In this chapter, we discuss findings from a project that sought to identify the socio-technical imaginaries of ADM and AI in health in Australia, comparing “actually existing ADM” with proposed imaginaries of the futures of ADM. We mapped how emerging health technologies are discussed in industry reports and websites. Our findings reveal that these complex assemblages of people, objects, data, spaces, systems, promises, expectations, and proximities generate a number of ethical issues and power dynamics.

documents.abstract: This article aimed to analyze the changes in reference services resulting from the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and generative AI, identifying ethical, conceptual, and operational challenges, as well as the new skills and educational guidelines required for information professionals. It used a qualitative, exploratory, and descriptive bibliographic and documentary research method, based on contemporary literature on Information Science, information mediation, and emerging technologies in education. It highlights that automation and conversational assistants (like chatbots and recommendation systems) streamline operational processes and speed up access and personalization of searches; however, human mediation remains essential to ensure information literacy, critical evaluation of sources, accuracy in data retrieval, and mitigation of algorithmic hallucinations. It can be concluded that artificial intelligence doesn’t replace the librarian, but rather reshapes their role for strategic tasks, ethical oversight, and digital curation, showing that the future of reference services lies in the convergence of technological efficiency and humanized mediation.

Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) has become an increasingly important concern in India as industrialisation, urbanisation, technological development, and the expansion of employment continue to reshape the world of work. Workplace safety is no longer limited to preventing machinery-related accidents or physical injuries. Workers may face chemical exposure, biological risks, unsafe equipment, poor ergonomics, occupational diseases, excessive working hours, workplace violence, stress, and other psychosocial risks. These concerns exist across sectors, including construction, manufacturing, mining, chemical industries, agriculture, informal employment, and healthcare. India has developed a substantial legal framework for protecting workers, culminating in the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, which came into force on November 21, 2025. However, the existence of legislation alone cannot guarantee safe working conditions. The continuing occurrence of workplace accidents, under-reporting of occupational diseases, inadequate safety infrastructure, and institutional failures demonstrate the need for stronger implementation and accountability. Recent attention to workplace safety following the R.G. Kar Medical College incident has further shown that occupational safety also includes dignity, security, gender-sensitive protection, and psychological well-being. The central concern, therefore, should be to move from a culture that reacts to accidents towards one that identifies and prevents risks before workers are harmed. Keywords: Occupational Safety and Health; Occupational Hazards; Workplace Safety; Occupational Diseases; Worker Protection.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: This working paper sets out the theoretical foundations of the Operational Continuity and Turnaround Architecture (OCTA), a domain-free quantitative model for predicting, detecting and arresting operational collapse in complex sociotechnical systems. The two core constructs are the Dependency Cascade Index (DCI), which measures the ratio of active dependencies to remaining recovery capacity in real time, and the intervention window W(t), which measures the time remaining before DCI crosses the irreversible collapse threshold. Together these constructs enable early detection of cascade propagation and provide a formal basis for turnaround intervention before collapse becomes irreversible. The model is validated primarily in civil aviation, using GNSS interference and ADS-B signal degradation as observable proxies for DCI dynamics. Domain-independence of the W(t) mechanism is demonstrated across banking and financial systems, automotive supply chains, nuclear energy, maritime operations, power grid infrastructure and healthcare systems. This working paper is part of a PhD research programme at Cranfield University. The commercial implementation of OCTA is developed through the TYRAXE technology stack (AIX, LINK, FLOW). Patent pending.

This study investigates how a structured “paper-first” approach can support cognitive engagement during artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted academic work in higher education. Growing reliance on generative AI has increased concerns about surface-level learning, trial-and-error prompting, and reduced student ownership of academic writing. Using a two-year design-based research approach involving nine iterative cycles, the study developed and refined a framework that required students to construct manual logic diagrams before engaging with AI tools and expert system environments. Participants included a six-member interdisciplinary design team and 150 communication for academic purposes students from the faculty of information and communications technology at a South African university. Data were collected through iterative observations and focus group interviews and analyzed using grounded theory and constant comparative analysis. Findings indicate that the framework supported more structured reasoning, reduced inefficient prompting behaviors, and improved students’ ability to identify weaknesses in their own arguments before digital interaction. Students also reported increased confidence and greater ownership of their academic work. The study argues that structured pre-AI planning activities can strengthen critical thinking and academic literacy by positioning AI as a support tool rather than a substitute for cognitive effort. The findings contribute practical guidance for educators seeking to integrate AI into higher education while preserving student agency and deep learning.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Transformasi digital mendorong organisasi mengintegrasikan Artificial Intelligence (AI) dan Digital Human Resource Management (Digital HRM) dalam proses pengelolaan sumber daya manusia. AI dapat membantu analisis data, penyaringan kandidat, pembelajaran, serta evaluasi kinerja, sedangkan Digital HRM mendukung digitalisasi administrasi dan layanan SDM melalui sistem informasi yang terintegrasi. Penelitian ini bertujuan mengkaji bagaimana AI dan Digital HRM berkontribusi terhadap efektivitas manajemen sumber daya manusia, sekaligus mengidentifikasi tantangan penerapannya. Artikel disusun melalui tinjauan literatur sistematis dengan fokus pada publikasi ilmiah tahun 2021–2025. Sumber ditelusuri melalui publikasi jurnal yang dapat diidentifikasi melalui DOI dan laman penerbit, dengan kata kunci terkait AI in HRM, digital HRM, e-HRM, HR technology, dan HRM effectiveness. Pemetaan awal literatur menunjukkan empat tema utama: efisiensi proses dan dukungan keputusan; penerimaan dan kesiapan organisasi; pengalaman serta peran profesional SDM; dan tata kelola yang bertanggung jawab. Literatur menunjukkan potensi peningkatan kecepatan proses, konsistensi layanan, dan dukungan keputusan, tetapi manfaat tersebut tidak terjadi secara otomatis. Kualitas data, kompetensi pengguna, transparansi algoritma, privasi, bias, serta kesesuaian teknologi dengan kebutuhan organisasi menjadi faktor penting. Kajian ini menyimpulkan bahwa AI dan Digital HRM sebaiknya diposisikan sebagai sarana pendukung strategi SDM, bukan pengganti pertimbangan manusia.

documents.abstract: University students increasingly use artificial intelligence tools for learning, decision-making, and academic work, making perceived AI dependence a relevant issue for public mental health and digital public health rather than only for educational technology. This three-wave time-lagged survey examined whether experiential avoidance functioned as a putative explanatory process linking perceived AI dependence with later anxiety symptoms and whether digital literacy moderated the tested pathways. Online survey data were collected from 1,451 university students with AI-use experience; perceived AI dependence, digital literacy, and baseline demographic variables were measured in January 2026, experiential avoidance was measured in March 2026, and anxiety symptoms were measured in June 2026. PLS-SEM results showed that experiential avoidance was strongly and positively associated with later anxiety symptoms (beta = 0.677, p < 0.001), whereas the direct association between perceived AI dependence and anxiety symptoms was not significant (beta = -0.030, p = 0.147); perceived AI dependence was negatively associated with experiential avoidance (beta = -0.114, p < 0.001), producing a statistically significant but theoretically unexpected negative time-ordered indirect association (beta = -0.077, p < 0.001), and digital literacy did not significantly moderate the tested pathways. The findings suggest that anxiety symptoms in AI-mediated learning contexts are closely linked to avoidance-related psychological processes, while the meaning of perceived AI dependence is context-dependent and should not be equated automatically with harmful use or clinical addiction; campus mental-health promotion should therefore integrate responsible AI education with support for psychological flexibility, uncertainty tolerance, and autonomous learning.

The advent of generative artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming academic production and confronting the social sciences with the challenge of preserving critical thinking in the face of mechanically generated content. This research examines the perceptions and practices of social science lecturers and students at Ecuadorian universities regarding the use of AI, together with their motivations, constraints and the institutional policies currently in force. A mixed-methods design was adopted, combining qualitative and quantitative approaches. The instruments comprised semi-structured interviews with lecturers and students at national and Ibero-American universities; a non-probabilistic survey of 200 students; and a content analysis of seven sets of regulations from universities in Ecuador, all aligned with the framework of competencies identified by UNESCO-IESALC. The results show a moderate-to-high level of AI use (mean = 3.68), explained by perceived usefulness and extrinsic motivation rather than ease of use, and a gap between the demand for regulation (4.00) and perceived regulatory clarity (3.21); only one of the seven universities has a policy formally designated as such, and ethics predominates over professional and disciplinary development. The study concludes that the governance of AI in Ecuadorian higher education requires an evaluative redesign and discipline-differentiated competencies.

documents.abstract: Aiming at weak communication network coverage and low-efficiency manual network optimization (NRO) troubleshooting in mountainous rural areas, this paper proposes an artificial intelligence (AI) assisted NRO approach, constructing a human-machine collaborative workflow: "AI simulation pre-judgment, data preliminary screening, engineer on-site recheck, closed-loop iterative optimization." AI leverages massive data processing for coverage simulation, poor-quality user mining, tidal traffic analysis, and geological hazard identification to narrow manual inspection scope; engineers conduct targeted rectification and feed measured data back to correct model deviations. This study selects typical mountainous townships in Hanzhong as pilot, integrating multi-source data including measurement reports (MR), base-station engineering parameters, traffic key performance indicators (KPI), user complaint tickets, and digital elevation model (DEM). AI pre-screening output 42 points to be checked; after on-site recheck, 14 false alarms were removed and 28 real problems confirmed. Optimization effects were compared across network quality, user perception, O&M workload, and hazard early-warning dimensions. Implementation constraints including model bias, outdated equipment, talent shortage, funding insufficiency, and data barriers are analyzed, with countermeasures proposed from operation mechanism, hardware iteration, talent cultivation, resource coordination, and data governance dimensions, providing reference for large-scale AI application in rural communication NRO.

Reinforcement Learning (RL) for Large Language Model (LLM) agents in multi-turn, long-horizon environments remains challenging due to inefficient action selection and repetitive behavioral patterns. In particular, agents often become trapped in high-confidence yet unproductive behaviors, repeatedly executing invalid actions or entering action loops that hinder task completion. We observe that these frequently violate environment preconditions, revealing a mismatch between the agent's representation of the internal state and the dynamics of the underlying environment. In addition, repetitive high-confidence actions lead to cyclical behaviors that provide little to no progress towards the goal. We argue that addressing these challenges requires more productive task-aligned exploration to improve the agent's understanding of environment dynamics. Motivated by intrinsic curiosity-driven exploration, we propose a conditional state-space exploration framework that balances task completion with intrinsic information-seeking behavior. Specifically, we introduce an intrinsic reward that penalizes actions whose observation duplicates prior state memory. This provides the benefit of reducing redundant behaviors and encouraging state-space coverage without relying on a general information-theoretic measure. Strong experimental results demonstrate that our approach substantially improves policy learning in multi-turn environments, mitigating invalid actions and repetitive loops.

Supplementary material for the paper "Consensus or Debate? Interactional Patterns of Idea Development with AI Peers in Collaborative Discussion" (under review).The document reproduces, verbatim, the prompts that drove the AI peer in a Wizard-of-Oz study of small-group discussions. A large language model (Gemini 2.5 Flash) periodically assessed the conversation with an assessment prompt and, when an intervention seemed warranted, drafted one with a generation prompt; a human Wizard then sent, edited or dismissed it. Two stances were compared: ConsensusBot, which synthesised ideas and moved the group toward agreement, and DebateBot, a devil's advocate that probed premature agreement and unchallenged claims. The prompts were configured for each stance, participant group (students, educators) and discussion topic, giving eight configurations. The document also gives the inputs, output formats, temperatures and token limits for each call.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: People increasingly confide their most dangerous thoughts to artificial intelligence (AI). Studies report that users disclose suicidal ideation more readily to conversational agents than to standard questionnaires or to other people, and platform data suggest that more than a million people each week discuss suicide with a single general-purpose chatbot. Yet this unprecedented volume of disclosure has not translated into proportionate protection, and some of the most serious harms associated with AI in mental health have occurred precisely within relationships of intense disclosure. This article proposes Pseudoparousia Theory (from the Greek pseudo-, false, and parousia, presence) to explain this paradox. The theory holds that disclosure seeks not only a listener but a presence: an other who is affected by what is disclosed, able to act on it, and continuous and accountable over time. Conversational AI produces the experience of presence – attention, responsiveness, apparent empathy, constant availability – without its substance. This counterfeit presence, or pseudoparousia, lowers the cost of disclosure for exactly the reasons that it removes disclosure’s protective consequences. The theory defines presence through three components (affectedness, agency, and continuity), distinguishes four configurations of witnessing (embodied presence, echo, deflection, and absence), formulates six propositions, and derives testable hypotheses, a measurement program, and implications for design, clinical practice, and regulation. Its central claim is that the decisive question for AI in mental health is not how accurately a system can detect distress, but whether presence can be transferred from the machine to a person in time.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Psychological and behavioral modeling turns cognition, emotion, and motivation into computable quantities that can be related to observable behavior. The field has moved from theory-driven rules to statistical machine learning, deep learning, large language models (LLMs), and foundation models of cognition, but methods are fragmented, results are seldom comparable, and the link between opaque predictors and psychological theory is unsettled. This structured narrative review, reported with a PRISMA-style selection flow and an explicit evidence-tier coding, frames the field as a multilevel system. It organizes research into five modeling classes (psychological states, behavioral capabilities, individual–environment interaction, individual dynamics, and group psychology), defined by unit of analysis, target, and direction of inference, and it positions system dynamics, in the stock–flow–feedback sense, as one model family within that scheme rather than as a synonym for dynamical-systems modeling. We score the computational readiness of the theories that supply model ontologies on two rubric-based axes, formal specification and measurement maturity, and compare model families by assumptions, data needs, interpretability, and failure modes. Four claims are defended, each with stated boundary conditions and counterexamples: theory readiness, not algorithmic capability, determines where theory-informed learning is feasible; the dominant use of models shifts from individual-level estimation to collective-level simulation without a parallel shift in validation; multilevel data, not model capacity, constrain cross-scale modeling; and readiness claims must be indexed to a graded evidence base. We catalogue datasets, including small-group, dyadic, and longitudinal-network resources, review applications in mental health, education, decision support, and emergency management with their evidentiary status made explicit, treat military use as an ethically bounded case, and turn five recurrent bottlenecks into research-practice recommendations paired, where possible, with testable predictions.

Existing steering benchmarks are built around simplified, isolated generation tasks and evaluate a single behavioral attribute under controlled settings that do not reflect the diversity and complexity of practical deployment. As a result, performance on these benchmarks provides only a limited picture of how steering methods perform in the real world. We therefore introduce RealControlBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating fine-grained steering of LLMs and LLM agents across diverse behavioral targets and interaction settings. RealControlBench extends steering evaluation beyond isolated generations to complex, execution-grounded, multi-turn agent interactions, covering five complementary dimensions: instruction-following control, agentic tool-use decision control, reasoning-performance steering, reasoning-length control, and trajectory-conditioned safety awareness. Rather than measuring steering success alone, the benchmark jointly evaluates target controllability and capability preservation, including instruction following, reasoning performance, and downstream agent utility and safety. It further examines whether steering effects remain specific and robust across prompt variations, domains, and model architectures. Our evaluation shows that existing steering methods remain unreliable across realistic control objectives: they often fail to consistently induce the intended behavior and can substantially degrade the model's underlying task performance. These results suggest that strong steering effects in controlled settings do not necessarily translate into reliable control in more realistic evaluations. By providing a unified, model-agnostic steering evaluation framework, RealControlBench aims to support the development of steering methods that are not only effective but also precise, robust, and useful in realistic AI deployments.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This article examines the reconfiguration of the civil liability regime governing the use and integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in international arbitration. Based on a dogmatic distinction between AI used as a professional support tool, on the one hand, and autonomous AI systems (such as the so-called “AI arbitrator”), on the other hand, this article evaluates the applicability of both fault-based (subjective) and strict (objective) liability regimes. The study analyzes the core elements of civil liability (generating act or wrong, compensable damage, and causal link) within the conduct of the main arbitration actors, particularly arbitrators and counsel, with particular emphasis on compliance with soft law and hard law frameworks, duties of transparency, confidentiality, and the fundamental principle prohibiting the delegation of adjudicative functions. The article concludes that while the assistive use of AI is governed by a fault-based liability centered on human oversight and professional diligence of the person using it, autonomous AI requires strict or hybrid liability models. Finally, it cautions against the risks of setting aside or refusing recognition of arbitral awards due to due process and public policy violations, wondering about a possible reinterpretation of traditional procedural principles such as iura novit curia.

Generative AI is reshaping how research software is written, reviewed, and maintained — and with it, is changing the role of the people who do that work. In March 2026, about three dozen leaders from across the global research software community gathered in Edinburgh for a 2.5-day workshop to confront this transformation directly: to share emerging practices, examine the risks alongside the opportunities, and begin building a coordinated community response. Working groups determined and addressed nine key areas where further work is needed to understand how generative AI is affecting the research software community and to develop policies, practices, and resources to respond to the changes generative AI is bringing: communicating with policymakers and institutional leadership about the need for continued investment in RSEs and generative AI tools to support RSE work; trade-offs between the costs/risks and benefits of generative AI for research software; changes to publishing, preserving, and crediting code creation and maintenance; verification and validation of research software; definitions of the RSE role; training needs from RSEs and the researcher community; management of RSE teams and OSS (Open-Source Software) communities; accessibility and responsible use of generative AI tools and resources; and collaboration in teams with AI in the mix. This talk will share the themes and output of the workshop with the broader RSE community, including opportunities to get involved in the dozens of activities that participants identified and prioritized for helping RSEs, funders, researchers, research institutions, governments, and others respond to the risks and opportunities from generative AI for research software.

Lasswell's five-question formula remains a durable frame for analyzing source, message, channel, audience and effect. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) underlying mass communication assumptions: intentional human sources, relatively static messages, channels as carries, audiences as receivers and effects as downstream outcomes. This conceptual paper argues for extension rather than abandonment. Its objectives are to examine the model’s analytical adequacy and develop an extension for generative communication. Using scholarship from AI-mediated communication, human-machine communication, algorithmic media, trust and synthetic content and accountability. research to illustrate how these systems can generate, revise, personalize messages (i.e. These competencies allow for the communication of agents that exist as a dispersed network, but ultimately moral agency lies with human and institutional figures. Critical comparative conceptual analysis relates this literature to Lasswell's five questions and integrates the resulting distinctions into a framework. The analysis identifies distributed communicative agency, synthetic and hybrid voice, intelligent mediation, audience co-participation and recursive effects. It distinguishes machine influence from human and institutional responsibility. The proposed framework makes trust appraisal, verification and accountability explicit, with transparency and provenance applying across all stages. Feedback connects outcomes to subsequent production and distribution. It is therefore required as an initial stage of analysis but in times and environments where the source, message and channel can be at least partially artificial, it becomes insufficient. The framework offers concepts for empirical research and practical guidance for documenting authorship, verifying claims and identifying responsible actors in journalism, education and public communication.

Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) has grown significantly since its introduction and inception in the late 1950s and has become interwoven into healthcare. Objective: This narrative review evaluates practice concerns and perceptions associated with the heightened demand for AI in healthcare, particularly as a cost-saving tool for nursing and providers. Methods: Online databases included PubMed and CINAHL. Boolean terminology included healthcare and AI, AI and nursing, as well as AI and ethics. Results were limited to complete online articles written within the previous five years. Initial searches yielded over 55,469 results. Results: Despite a growing push from federal agencies and hospital systems to incorporate their use, there is no definitive consensus on the application of AI in healthcare. This may cause harm to patients as AI tools are not consistently accurate, may misdiagnose, and have potential for "unconscious" bias. However, significant time and cost may be saved with care algorithm implementation. Conclusions: Careful evaluation and ethical analysis are warranted on a case-by-case basis prior to commencement. Nursing staff and healthcare providers are integral to the "care algorithm" and cannot be removed from direct patient care without potential harm.

documents.abstract: Personalised robot tutoring requires real-time pedagogical decision-making under uncertain and multimodal learner states. Existing intelligent tutoring and robot-assisted learning systems often rely on static rules, single-modality learner modelling, or short-term correctness-oriented optimisation, which limits their capacity to balance knowledge acquisition, engagement, retention, and safe embodied interaction. RL-Robotutor is presented as a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that integrates cognitive knowledge-tracing signals, facial-expression and gaze-derived affective cues, and behavioural interaction logs through transformer-based fusion. A PPO-trained meta-policy selects among specialised modules for learner assessment, curriculum adaptation, strategy selection, and reflective feedback, while a hybrid reward combines immediate learning performance, engagement, long-term learning gain, and safety. The evidence is reported by source: five public knowledge-tracing datasets assess the cognitive prediction component; controlled simulator experiments assess policy learning, reward ablation, and multimodal fusion; and a randomised robot-tutoring study assesses embodied interaction with 120 undergraduate participants. RL-Robotutor outperforms rule-based, flat reinforcement-learning, knowledge-tracing, and LLM-based comparators. In the human study, the learning gain is 0.62, compared with 0.40 for the rule-based robot condition. The full hybrid reward improves simulator learning gain by 19% over correctness-only optimisation, and full multimodal fusion improves simulator engagement by 17% over text-only modelling. Jetson Orin deployment achieves 48 ms inference latency with an absolute AUC reduction of 0.007, supporting real-time edge execution.

Over the years, the accumulation of vast amounts of safety data and information has not only enhanced our understanding of …

Safety alignment for large language models (LLMs) is primarily performed during post-training, while recent work has also begun incorporating safety data into pre-training. Yet safety can degrade when later training no longer includes safety data, and gains in safety often come at the cost of general capability. This tension suggests that safety and general reasoning should not be treated as separate training goals. We instead view safety as an LLM capability that can be learned through a reasoning structure shared with general tasks. Both require the model to understand intent or task goals, apply relevant knowledge, and reason about potential consequences. We introduce safety mid-training, a stage between pre-training and post-training that jointly develops safety and general reasoning through this shared structure. Given safety and utility prompts, the base model generates structured documents and reasoning traces that are then used for mid-training. Safety mid-training reduces average attack success rate (ASR) by 72% to 81% relative to Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B base models, while also improving general capability. The benefits persist through subsequent post-training. After general-only SFT, mid-trained models largely retain their safety, achieving lower ASR than the baselines without sacrificing general capability. They also retain safety under general-only GRPO without safety rewards, while subsequent RL reaches a better safety-utility frontier when initialized from the mid-trained models. Together, these results suggest that learning safety and general reasoning within a shared mid-training stage can reduce the safety-utility trade-off and make safety more robust to subsequent training.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative AI is reshaping how research software is developed. Tools and patterns ranging from “vibe coding” through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and autonomous agents now offer compelling productivity gains, but their adoption in scientific computing surfaces failure modes that general-purpose evaluation does not catch: silent unit conversions, violated conservation laws, hallucinated physics, loss of numerical precision, and quietly broken reproducibility. These failures share a signature: nothing visible goes wrong. The AI ecosystem itself is moving fast, leaving RSEs to make consequential integration decisions with little shared vocabulary or principled guidance. This talk introduces Scientific Agentic Engineering, the central contribution of an in-progress 2026 Better Scientific Software (BSSw) Fellowship: a tool-agnostic methodology for integrating AI agents into high-stakes scientific software workflows. The framework defines how agents, scientific skills, and MCP servers should be structured around validation loops, explicit human-in-the-loop checkpoints, and domain-specific safeguards. Every task moves through a short workflow (frame, plan and critique, implement, verify), with decisions recorded throughout, and the framework maps each documented failure mode to the stage where it is cheapest to catch. The intent is not to recommend any particular AI tool but to articulate foundational concepts that remain valid as the underlying technology changes. I will share three artifacts from the fellowship: The Framework (published July 2026). Shared vocabulary, its principles and workflow, structural guidance on where safeguards live, and a pattern catalog of named practices, each tied to the failure it counters. The Reference Workflow. A structured exercise in which RSEs use AI tools to build a small weather-model error-statistics application, applying the framework to avoid the failure modes it documents. The Community Repository. A curated starter set of scientific MCP server templates, agent skills such as unit checkers and conservation-law validators, and agent configuration examples, designed to be starting points for the community to adapt to a variety of scientific domains. These artifacts are by design community resources, and broader adoption is the explicit aim of the remaining milestones, which include an interactive online tutorial series comparing purpose-built scientific agents with general-purpose tools, a recorded live workshop published for asynchronous access, and a BSSw.io blog post directing the community to the project’s resources. This work engages the conference theme directly by advancing AI-assisted scientific software development from ad-hoc experimentation toward a disciplined, transferable engineering practice.

Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems can plan multi-step tasks, use external tools, retrieve information, andtake actions with limited human intervention. These capabilities create security and privacy risks beyond those found inconventional question-answering systems. An agent may encounter malicious instructions in retrieved content, misuse anauthorized tool, expose confidential context, retain unnecessary personal data, or continue a harmful action through a chain ofotherwise ordinary steps. This paper presents a risk-aware framework for analysing these challenges across the agent lifecycle. Itorganizes the main risks into instruction and prompt injection, excessive agency, insecure tool integration, data leakage, identityand access-control weaknesses, memory risks, and insufficient monitoring. The proposed approach combines least-privilegepermissions, separation of trusted instructions from untrusted data, explicit approval for high-impact actions, privacy-awarememory, output validation, and audit logging. A staged evaluation plan is described using threat scenarios and measurablesecurity and privacy indicators. This paper is a design-oriented study and does not claim experimental results or a deployedsecurity product. Its central argument is that agentic AI should be treated as a socio-technical system whose safety depends on themodel, tools, data, permissions, and surrounding operational controls
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Autonomous driving systems increasingly depend on simulation for scalable training, yet the transfer of learned policies to unseen real-world environments remains a central obstacle. This paper examines sim-to-real transfer through the lens of adaptive post-training, understood not merely as a final fine-tuning step but as a socio-technical capability embedded in the lifecycle of autonomous vehicle deployment. The argument is that unseen environments expose structural limits in simulation-based development because they combine perceptual novelty, behavioral ambiguity, infrastructure irregularity, and governance uncertainty. Adaptive post-training can narrow these gaps by recalibrating representations, control policies, and safety constraints after initial training, using limited field data, targeted simulations, and operational feedback. However, such adaptation also introduces new system-level trade-offs involving architectural complexity, verification burden, data governance, fairness, sustainability, and accountability. The paper develops a conceptual framework for analyzing these trade-offs and connects them to practical concerns in autonomous driving, including operational design domains, edge-case exposure, model auditing, and infrastructure dependence. It also compares autonomous driving with robotics, aviation, and large-scale machine learning systems to clarify how post-training changes reliability engineering and policy expectations. The conclusion is that adaptive post-training is necessary but insufficient by itself; it must be paired with transparent validation, continuous monitoring, and institutional mechanisms that distribute responsibility across manufacturers, operators, regulators, and affected communities. The paper contributes a system-level research agenda for making sim-to-real transfer robust, equitable, and sustainable in unseen environments.

Burnout syndrome is an occupational health concern among professionals working in Intensive Care Units (ICUs), settings characterized by complex care and high physical and emotional demands. This study aimed to analyze the impacts of burnout on these professionals and its relationship with patient safety and quality of care. An integrative literature review was conducted using a qualitative, descriptive, and exploratory approach, with searches in SciELO, PubMed, the Virtual Health Library, and Google Scholar. Eligible articles were published between 2015 and 2025, available in full text, written in Portuguese, English, or Spanish, and related to the study topic. The analysis identified workload overload, long working hours, staff shortages, frequent exposure to suffering, and insufficient institutional support as factors associated with burnout. Occupational exhaustion was associated with impaired attention, communication, and decision-making, with implications for quality of care and patient safety. Prevention strategies included adequate staffing, psychological support, professional recognition, and improved working conditions. It was concluded that early recognition of burnout and the adoption of institutional prevention measures are essential to promoting professionals’ mental health and ensuring safe, humanized care in intensive care settings.

The emergence of artificial intelligence algorithms has surprised all scientific fields. The education system, for example, is impacted by the possibility of perhaps superficial and certainly very rapid learning of difficult theories that previously took years to master. The science system, on the other hand, besides being impacted by the possibilities, is above all optimistic about the advances. The economic system also sees marked changes. But the legal system is, in a way, apprehensive considering the ethical and normative aspects. The first point relates to decisions. The second point relates specifically to norms and structures of expectations. No one can predict what the consequences will be. But everyone can say that the systems are already revealing great changes and evolutions. Thus, the question arises as to what evolutions have already occurred in the legal system with artificial intelligence.

This study aims to describe students’motivation toward the use of the Alef Platform, an AI-based adaptive learning system, in English vocabulary learning. Vocabulary mastery is a fundamental yet often challenging aspect of English learning for secondary school students, and technology-enhanced learning platforms are increasingly used to address low learning motivation. This research employed a convergent mixed-methods design, combining a validated 24-item Likert-scale questionnaire administered to 70 students with semi-structured interviews and classroom observations involving nine purposively selected students. The questionnaire measured three motivational dimensions: intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, and perceived usefulness. The results show that students' overall motivation toward the use of the Alef Platform falls into the Very High category (M = 4.20; Very High = 4.21–5.00 on the study's 1.00–5.00 five-point interpretive scale), with intrinsic motivation as the strongest dimension (M = 4.28), followed by perceived usefulness (M = 4.24) and extrinsic motivation (M = 4.09). Qualitative findings reveal that students experienced enjoyment, curiosity, and a sense of achievement while using the platform, while teacher facilitation, grades, and the platform's reward system remained meaningful sources of extrinsic motivation; these qualitative findings converge with and help explain the quantitative results, particularly the comparatively lower extrinsic motivation score. The study concludes that adaptive digital platforms such as Alef are associated with higher motivation in EFL vocabulary learning when implemented consistently and supported by active teacher facilitation.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in English writing instruction to support idea generation, drafting, revision, and editing. However, research on vocational high school students’ perceptions of AI-supported English writing in Indonesia remains limited. This study examined students’ perceptions of AI applications in English writing at SMK Negeri 2 Bengkulu City. A descriptive quantitative survey involved 70 tenth-grade students selected purposively based on their prior experience using AI applications. Data were collected using an adapted 20-item questionnaire covering motivation, learning quality, AI value, cognitive learning, affective learning, and course quality. Descriptive analysis examined mean scores and percentages to determine students’ perceptions across the six dimensions. The findings revealed a very high overall perception of AI-supported English writing learning (M = 4.22; 84.4%). Course quality received the highest rating (M = 4.26; 85.2%), whereas cognitive learning recorded the lowest (M = 4.16; 83.2%). These findings indicate that students generally perceived AI positively as a supportive tool for English writing instruction. The results highlight the perceived educational value of AI while underscoring the need to strengthen its contribution to students’ cognitive engagement and independent writing development.

Mining is one of the most hazardous industries due to the presence of underground operations, heavy machinery, explosive materials, dust, toxic gases, and challenging environmental conditions. Despite significant advancements in mining technology and safety equipment, workplace accidents continue to occur, with human factors being a major contributing cause. Human factors refer to the physical, psychological, behavioral, and organizational characteristics that influence workers' ability to perform tasks safely and efficiently. This study examines the major human factors affecting mine safety performance, including training and competency, fatigue, communication, safety culture, leadership, stress, risk perception, experience, and organizational management. The report is based on a review of published research, safety guidelines, and reports from organizations such as the Directorate General of Mines Safety (DGMS), the International Labour Organization (ILO), the International Council on Mining and Metals (ICMM), and the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA). The study highlights how inadequate training, poor communication, excessive workload, weak supervision, and unsafe work practices contribute to accidents, injuries, and reduced operational efficiency. The findings indicate that improving human factors through continuous training, effective leadership, strong safety culture, fatigue management, employee participation, and regular safety audits can significantly reduce accident rates and enhance overall mine safety performance. The report concludes that integrating human factor principles into mine safety management systems is essential for creating a safer working environment, improving productivity, and ensuring the long-term sustainability of mining operations.

documents.abstract: ObjectiveThis study examined whether multidimensional recurrence quantification analysis (MdRQA) metrics derived from team heart rate data predict team performance and team workload under varied team and task demands.BackgroundAssessing team performance in operational environments is challenging. Traditional approaches require task interruptions or ground-truth data that are often unavailable. Physiological sensing offers a less-intrusive approach, yet most applications aggregate individual-level data or rely on simple pairwise metrics that do not represent how coupling is organized across the whole team. MdRQA instead embeds multivariate time series into a shared phase space, but evidence linking MdRQA metrics to team outcomes remains limited and mixed.MethodTwenty triads completed a cooperative virtual reality choice reaction time task across four conditions manipulating interdependence and time pressure. MdRQA metrics (percent determinism, average diagonal line length, diagonal line entropy) were extracted from heart rate interbeat interval data. Linear mixed-effects models tested whether these metrics predicted self-reported team workload and team performance outcomes including sensitivity and response bias from signal detection theory.ResultsLonger sustained coupling predicted increased sensitivity and fewer errors, while greater entropy predicted poorer performance. Higher determinism and lower entropy predicted a more liberal response bias. MdRQA metrics did not predict perceived workload beyond condition effects.ConclusionMdRQA metrics reflect joint physiological dynamics and predict performance outcomes in triads beyond the effects of task demands alone.ApplicationContinuously computed physiological coupling metrics may serve as less-intrusive, real-time proxies for team performance in operational environments where traditional assessment is infeasible.
topics: Heart Rate Variability and Autonomic Control
